claim: Extracellular single-unit recordings were obtained from LGN neurons and from the retinotopically-aligned region of V1 in four awake adult female Dutch-Belted rabbits.
source: Extracellular single-unit recordings were obtained from LGN neurons and from the retinotopically-aligned region of V1 in four awake adult female Dutch-Belted rabbits.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental methods used, describing the recording procedures and animal subjects.

claim: Three 'rules' regulate thalamocortical connectivity between LGN neurons and layer 4 fast-spike inhibitory interneurons.
source: We show that three 'rules' regulate this connectivity.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental findings demonstrating three conditions that govern connectivity.

claim: The first rule concerns the precision of retinotopic alignment between LGN neurons and L4 SINs.
source: These rules concern: (1) the precision of retinotopic alignment
evidence: This is stated explicitly in the abstract and demonstrated through experimental data in Figure 2A.

claim: The second rule concerns the amplitude of the postsynaptic local field potential elicited near the interneuron by spikes of the LGN neuron.
source: These rules concern: (1) the precision of retinotopic alignment, (2) the amplitude of the postsynaptic local field potential elicited near the interneuron by spikes of the LGN neuron
evidence: This is stated explicitly in the abstract and demonstrated through experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: The third rule concerns the interneuron's response latency to strong, synchronous LGN input.
source: These rules concern: (1) the precision of retinotopic alignment, (2) the amplitude of the postsynaptic local field potential elicited near the interneuron by spikes of the LGN neuron, and (3) the interneuron's response latency to strong, synchronous LGN input.
evidence: This is stated explicitly in the abstract and demonstrated through experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Virtually all first-order fast-spike interneurons receive input from nearly all LGN axons that synapse nearby, regardless of their visual response properties.
source: We found that virtually all first-order fast-spike interneurons receive input from nearly all LGN axons that synapse nearby, regardless of their visual response properties.
evidence: This is supported by cross-correlation analysis data showing high connectivity rates (40/41 cases in Figure 4C).

claim: Neighboring regular-spiking neurons do not show the same promiscuous connectivity pattern as fast-spike interneurons.
source: This was not the case for neighboring regular-spiking neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figure 5 showing only ~11% connectivity for regular-spiking neurons.

claim: The proportion of connected LGN-SIN pairs is high (~73%) when alignment is within ½ of the diameter of the LGN RF center.
source: The proportion of connected pairs is high (31/42 cell pairs, ~73%) when alignment is within ½ of the diameter of the LGN RF center
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A with specific numerical data.

claim: The proportion of connected LGN-SIN pairs drops off precipitously when misaligned by > ½ of a RF diameter.
source: drops off precipitously when misaligned by > ½ of a RF diameter.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and stated in the text describing the relationship between alignment and connectivity.

claim: 11 of 42 (~26%) highly-aligned LGN/SIN pairs (where RF centers separated by <½ of an LGN RF diameter) showed no signs of synaptic connectivity.
source: Thus, 11 of 42 (~26%) highly-aligned LGN/SIN pairs (where RF centers separated by <½ of an LGN RF diameter) showed no signs of synaptic connectivity.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results with specific numerical data.

claim: Precise retinotopic alignment is a necessary but not sufficient condition for synaptic connectivity between LGN neurons and L4 SINs.
source: Importantly, however, although precise retinotopic alignment was a necessary correlate of synaptic connectivity, it was not sufficient.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that some well-aligned pairs are not connected.

claim: LGN-SIN synaptic connectivity does not depend on similarity of ON/OFF response properties.
source: We found that neither similarity of LGN and SIN ON/OFF responses, nor similarity of sustained/transient responses was a significant factor in predicting the synaptic connectivity of retinotopically-aligned LGN/SIN pairs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the example in Figure 2 and statistical analysis showing no significant relationship.

claim: LGN-SIN synaptic connectivity does not depend on similarity of sustained/transient response properties.
source: We found that neither similarity of LGN and SIN ON/OFF responses, nor similarity of sustained/transient responses was a significant factor in predicting the synaptic connectivity of retinotopically-aligned LGN/SIN pairs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the example in Figure 2 and statistical analysis.

claim: The probability of observing connection in pairs where both ON/OFF and sustained/transient parameters were similar did not significantly differ from pairs where both parameters were dissimilar (p=0.769).
source: Moreover, the probability of observing the connection in pairs where both parameters were similar did not significantly differ from pairs where both parameters were dissimilar (X2 test, p=0.769).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical test results.

claim: Six of the 11 cases in which no synaptic connectivity was observed despite excellent retinotopic alignment can be accounted for by a very weak (or absent) LGN input to the vicinity of the SIN under study.
source: Thus, 6 of the 11 cases in which no synaptic connectivity was observed, despite excellent retinotopic alignment, can be accounted for by a very weak (or absent) LGN input to the vicinity of the SIN under study.
evidence: This is based on analysis of spike-triggered LFP amplitudes shown in Figure 3D.

claim: None of the SINs responding at synaptic latencies of >3 ms to electrical stimulation of the thalamus were synaptically connected to their paired and well-aligned LGN neuron.
source: None of the SINs responding at synaptic latencies of >3 ms to electrical stimulation of the thalamus were synaptically connected to their paired and well-aligned LGN neuron
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and stated explicitly in the text.

claim: 31/37 of the SINs showing synaptic latencies < 3 ms were connected to their paired LGN neuron.
source: (31/37 of the SINs showing synaptic latencies < 3 ms were connected).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results with specific numerical data.

claim: SINs with long synaptic latencies to electrical stimulation of the LGN (>3 ms) responded at longer latencies to visual stimulation than did those that responded at shorter synaptic latencies (<3 ms) (35.69 ± 1.78 ms vs. 25.77 ± 0.38 ms, respectively, p<0.001).
source: Notably, SINs with long synaptic latencies to electrical stimulation of the LGN (>3 ms) also responded at longer latencies to visual stimulation than did those that responded at shorter synaptic latencies (<3 ms) (Figure 4B, 35.69 ± 1.78 ms vs. 25.77 ± 0.38 ms, respectively, p<0.001)
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical comparison with specific values and significance level.

claim: The spike duration of long-latency SINs did not differ from those of the other SINs (0.467 ± 0.022 ms vs. 0.449 ± 0.022 ms, p=0.337).
source: Importantly, the spike duration of these long-latency SINs did not differ from those of the other SINs (0.467 ± 0.022 ms vs. 0.449 ± 0.022 ms, p=0.337).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical comparison with specific values and significance level.

claim: 31/32 well-aligned LGN-SIN cases were synaptically connected provided that they received a measurable postsynaptic input from the LGN (spike-triggered post-synaptic LFP amplitude >1 μV) and the synaptic latency to electrical stimulation of the LGN was <3 ms.
source: Thus, 31/32 well-aligned LGN-SIN cases were synaptically connected provided that (1) they received a measurable postsynaptic input from the LGN input (spike-triggered post-synaptic LFP amplitude >1 μV), and (2) the synaptic latency to electrical stimulation of the LGN was <3 ms.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results showing the predictive power of the three rules.

claim: Only three of 28 regular-spiking neurons located near a SIN that was synaptically connected to an LGN neuron received a functional input from the same LGN neuron (~11%).
source: Only three of these neurons (Figure 5A–B) received a functional input from the same LGN neuron (~11%)
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results with specific numerical data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The spike-triggered LFP generated by the LGN neuron recorded at the site of non-SINs was similar, albeit somewhat lower in amplitude than that measured at the site of the connected SIN (7.32 ± 0.59 μV and 8.72 ± 0.69 μV, respectively, p=0.023).
source: despite the fact that the spike-triggered LFP generated by the LGN neuron (recorded at the site of this non-SIN) was similar, albeit somewhat lower in amplitude than that measured at the site of the connected SIN (Figure 5B, 7.32 ± 0.59 μV and 8.72 ± 0.69 μV, respectively, p=0.023, paired t test).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical comparison with specific values and significance level.

claim: Non-SINs were 'regular-spiking', having considerably longer-duration spikes (0.921 ± 0.028 ms) than the neighboring connected SINs (0.455 ± 0.022 ms, p<0.001).
source: These non-SINs were 'regular-spiking', having considerably longer-duration spikes (0.921 ± 0.028 ms) than the neighboring connected SINs (0.455 ± 0.022 ms, p<0.001, Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical comparison with specific values and significance level.

claim: Retinal afferents make profuse retinogeniculate connections early during development but the connections are dramatically pruned at later developmental stages.
source: In thalamus, each retinal afferent makes profuse retinogeniculate connections early during development but the connections are dramatically pruned at later developmental stages leaving only a small subset of neurons connected to the same retinal afferent (Hamos et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Hamos et al., 1987).

claim: Thalamic axons are dramatically pruned during cortical development leaving only a subset of neurons connected to the same thalamic axon in the mature visual cortex.
source: Similarly, thalamic axons are dramatically pruned during cortical development leaving only a subset of neurons connected to the same thalamic axon in the mature visual cortex (Alonso et al., 2001; Taylor et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The specificity of thalamocortical connectivity differs for different classes of neurons in layer 4 of sensory neocortex.
source: However, the specificity of thalamocortical (TC) connectivity differs for different classes of neurons in layer 4 (L4) of sensory neocortex.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the subsequent discussion and citations.

claim: Synaptic connectivity between cells of the lateral geniculate nucleus and simple cells of the feline visual cortex is highly dependent on precise retinotopic alignment and similarity of receptive field properties.
source: For example, synaptic connectivity between cells of the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) and simple cells of the feline visual cortex (V1) is highly dependent on precise retinotopic alignment, but also requires a similarity of a number of receptive field (RF) properties of the thalamic inputs and cortical target neurons (Alonso et al., 2001; Hirsch and Martinez, 2006; Sedigh-Sarvestani et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The specificity of LGN-simple cell connectivity results in a relatively low connection probability between retinotopically-aligned LGN neurons and L4 simple cells.
source: This specificity results in a relatively low connection probability between retinotopically-aligned LGN neurons and L4 simple cells, and accounts, in part, for the orientation and direction selectivity of visual cortical simple cells (Alonso et al., 2001; Lien and Scanziani, 2018; Sedigh-Sarvestani et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and logical inference.

claim: The probability of a synaptic connection between a TC neuron and a topographically aligned cortical fast-spike inhibitory neuron is much higher than for simple cells.
source: By contrast, the probability of a synaptic connection between a TC neuron and a topographically aligned cortical fast-spike inhibitory neuron is much higher.
evidence: This is supported by subsequent citations and data.

claim: A connection probability of ~2/3 is seen between ventrobasal thalamic neurons and putative fast-spike interneurons in the aligned somatosensory cortex of rabbits.
source: For example, a connection probability of ~2/3 is seen between ventrobasal thalamic neurons and putative fast-spike interneurons (suspected inhibitory interneurons, SINs) in the aligned somatosensory cortex of rabbits (Swadlow and Gusev, 2002) and rats (Bruno and Simons, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A connection probability of ~2/3 is seen between ventrobasal thalamic neurons and putative fast-spike interneurons in the aligned somatosensory cortex of rats.
source: For example, a connection probability of ~2/3 is seen between ventrobasal thalamic neurons and putative fast-spike interneurons (suspected inhibitory interneurons, SINs) in the aligned somatosensory cortex of rabbits (Swadlow and Gusev, 2002) and rats (Bruno and Simons, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In cat visual cortex, inhibitory cells respond to thalamic inputs with less selectivity than do the presumptive spiny simple cells.
source: In cat visual cortex, these inhibitory cells also respond to thalamic inputs with less selectivity than do the (presumptive) spiny simple cells (Sedigh-Sarvestani et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The three rules generate a highly accurate prediction (in 41 of 42 cases) of whether an LGN-SIN pair will be synaptically connected.
source: Together, these rules generate a highly accurate prediction (in 41 of 42 cases) of whether an LGN-SIN pair will be synaptically connected.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results with specific numerical data.

claim: The dense, highly divergent/convergent TC network resulting from the three rules is consistent with the broadly tuned RF properties of many fast-spike inhibitory cortical neurons.
source: Moreover, the dense, highly divergent/convergent TC network that results from the application of these 'rules' is consistent with the broadly tuned RF properties of many fast-spike inhibitory cortical neurons (Bruno and Simons, 2002; Hirsch et al., 2003; Nowak et al., 2008; Swadlow and Gusev, 2002; Zhuang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and logical inference from the current data.

claim: The connectivity pattern is consistent with the fast, potent, and broadly tuned feed-forward inhibition onto L4 spiny cells.
source: It is also consistent with the fast, potent, and broadly tuned feed-forward inhibition onto L4 spiny cells (Bagnall et al., 2011; Cruikshank et al., 2007; Gabernet et al., 2005; Miller et al., 2001a; Miller et al., 2001b; Swadlow, 2003; Taylor et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and logical inference from the current data.

claim: 50 concentric LGN neurons and 47 L4 SINs (64 LGN-SIN pairs) were studied.
source: We studied the functional connectivity between 50 concentric LGN neurons and 47 L4 SINs (64 LGN-SIN pairs) that had RFs aligned, to various extents, with those of the LGN RFs.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the sample size in the study.

claim: SINs were identified by the high-frequency spike discharge elicited by electrical stimulation of the thalamus (3 + spikes elicited at frequencies of >600 Hz).
source: As described in Methods, SINs were identified by the high-frequency spike discharge elicited by electrical stimulation of the thalamus (3 + spikes elicited at frequencies of >600 Hz).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental method for identifying SINs.

claim: SINs had spikes of very short duration.
source: SINs also had spikes of very short duration.
evidence: This is a direct statement of an observed characteristic of SINs.

claim: LGN concentric neurons yield only ON-center or OFF-center responses at short latencies.
source: By definition, LGN concentric neurons yield only ON-center or OFF-center responses at short latencies.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about LGN concentric neurons.

claim: The RFs of SINs consist of highly overlapping ON and OFF response zones, which usually occur at similar amplitudes and latencies.
source: By contrast, the RFs of SINs consists of highly overlapping ON and OFF response zones, which usually occur at similar amplitudes and latencies (Zhuang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and the current data.

claim: Short-latency, brief increases in spike probability are a hallmark of TC synaptic connectivity as measured by extracellular cross-correlation of spike trains.
source: Such short-latency, brief increases in spike probability are a hallmark of TC synaptic connectivity as measured by extracellular cross-correlation of spike trains (e.g. Reid and Alonso, 1995; Tanaka, 1983; Swadlow and Gusev, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work establishing this methodological principle.

claim: The efficacy of the LGN-SIN connection shown in Figure 1F was 2.6%.
source: The 'efficacy' of this connection (an index of the probability that an LGN spike will elicit a SIN spike) was 2.6%.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a measured value for a specific example.

claim: Retinotopic alignment was a dominant factor governing synaptic connectivity between LGN concentric cells and L4 SINs.
source: Retinotopic alignment was a dominant factor governing synaptic connectivity between LGN concentric cells and L4 SINs.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2A and the statistical analysis.

claim: The high connection probability between aligned LGN neurons and SINs implies a very high degree of divergence from single LGN neurons to multiple aligned SINs.
source: This implies a very high degree of divergence from single LGN neurons to multiple aligned SINs, and convergence from multiple LGN neurons to individual retinotopically-aligned L4 SINs.
evidence: This is inferred from the high connection probability data.

claim: The high connection probability between aligned LGN neurons and SINs implies a high degree of convergence from multiple LGN neurons to individual retinotopically-aligned L4 SINs.
source: This implies a very high degree of divergence from single LGN neurons to multiple aligned SINs, and convergence from multiple LGN neurons to individual retinotopically-aligned L4 SINs.
evidence: This is inferred from the high connection probability data.

claim: TC neurons can differ greatly in the overall synaptic drive that they produce at different depths within L4.
source: TC neurons can differ greatly in the overall synaptic drive that they produce at different depths within L4 (Humphrey et al., 1985; Jin et al., 2008; Stoelzel et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Even neighboring LGN neurons may selectively target deep vs. superficial portions of L4.
source: Even neighboring LGN neurons may selectively target deep vs. superficial portions of L4 and some may not even project to V1 (e.g. interneurons).
evidence: This is supported by citations and general knowledge about LGN projections.

claim: Differences in synaptic drive at different cortical depths are reflected by the amplitude of the spike-triggered LFPs and/or current source density profiles generated by the spikes of single thalamic neurons.
source: When recording in vivo, such differences are reflected by the amplitude of the spike-triggered LFPs and/or current source density (CSD) profiles generated by the spikes of single thalamic neurons at different cortical depths (Jin et al., 2008; Jin et al., 2011; Stoelzel et al., 2008; Swadlow and Gusev, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work establishing this methodological principle.

claim: Long-latency SINs represent a different sub-class of fast-spike inhibitory interneuron in L4 that is connected to the thalamus in a different manner than short-latency SINs.
source: Together, these data support the notion that these 'long-latency' SINs represent a different sub-class of fast-spike inhibitory interneuron in L4 that is connected to the thalamus in a different manner than are those that respond at short synaptic latencies to LGN stimulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the data on latencies, connectivity patterns, and response properties.

claim: Recent studies in several cortical systems indicate that fast-spiking parvalbumin-expressing interneurons may be divisible into multiple functional subclasses.
source: Similarly, recent studies in several cortical systems indicate that fast-spiking parvalbumin-expressing interneurons may be divisible into multiple functional subclasses (Dávid et al., 2007; Garcia-Junco-Clemente et al., 2019; Shin and Moore, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Long-latency SINs have RFs that are indistinguishable from those of SINs which receive strong monosynaptic LGN input.
source: Surprisingly, these 'long-latency' SINs, which seem to lack significant monosynaptic input from the LGN have RF that are indistinguishable from those of SINs which do receive strong monosynaptic LGN input.
evidence: This is based on comparison of RF properties between the two SIN subclasses.

claim: L4 SINs in rabbit V1 can be divided into two classes based on their latency to electrical stimulation of the LGN: short-latency SINs (<2 ms) and long-latency SINs (>3 ms).
source: L4 SINs in rabbit V1 can be divided into two classes: those that respond at short latencies to strong electrical stimulation of the LGN (<2 ms, short-latency SINs), and those that respond at long latencies (>3 ms, long-latency SINs, Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on the distribution of latencies shown in Figure 4.

claim: The RFs of short-latency and long-latency SINs are virtually identical, consisting of overlapping ON and OFF zones, poor or no orientation/direction selectivity, and non-linear responses to drifting visual gratings.
source: Aside from the latency of the visual response, the RFs of these two cell classes are virtually identical, consisting of overlapping ON and OFF zones, and poor or no orientation/direction selectivity, and non-linear responses to drifting visual gratings.
evidence: This is based on comparison of RF properties between the two SIN subclasses.

claim: Most regular-spiking neurons (non-SINs) in L4 have 'simple' RFs consisting of one or more spatially separate ON and/or OFF zones, marked orientation/direction selectivity, and linear responses to drifting visual gratings.
source: By contrast, most regular-spiking neurons (non-SINs) in L4 have 'simple' RFs consisting of one or more spatially separate ON and/or OFF zones, marked orientation/direction selectivity, and linear responses to drifting visual gratings (Zhuang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Virtually all short-latency (first-order) L4 SINs receive a highly convergent input from virtually all of the LGN axons that synapse in their vicinity.
source: Our results show that, virtually all of the short-latency (first-order) L4 SINs receives a highly convergent input from virtually all of the LGN axons that synapse in their vicinity (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on the connectivity data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Short-latency SINs receive monosynaptic input from ON- and OFF-center LGN axons, as well as from LGN cells with both sustained and transient response properties.
source: Thus, the short-latency SINs receive monosynaptic input from ON- and OFF-center LGN axons, as well as from LGN cells with both sustained and transient response properties.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing lack of selectivity in connectivity based on these properties.

claim: The overlapping ON and OFF responding, and the broadly tuned response properties of short-latency SINs are expected to result from promiscuous TC input.
source: The overlapping ON and OFF responding, and the broadly tuned response properties of these SINs are what might be expected to result from such a promiscuous TC input.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the connectivity pattern and RF properties.

claim: There is little evidence for LGN axons with long conduction times in rabbit, as the vast majority of LGN neurons have TC conduction times of <2 ms (~98%).
source: Notably, there is little evidence for LGN axons with long conduction times in rabbit, as the vast majority of LGN neurons have TC conduction times of <2 ms (~98%, Stoelzel et al., 2008; Swadlow and Weyand, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In L4 of somatosensory barrel cortex, fast-spike interneurons receive a powerful and highly convergent input from neighboring spiny (regular-spiking) neurons.
source: Thus, in L4 of somatosensory barrel cortex, fast-spike interneurons receive a powerful and highly convergent input from neighboring spiny (regular-spiking) neurons.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent citation.

claim: The input from spiny to fast-spike neurons in barrel cortex is twice as strong and seven times more probable than is the input to other neighboring spiny neurons.
source: This input (spiny to fast-spike) is twice as strong and seven times more probable than is the input to other neighboring spiny neurons (Beierlein et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Regular-spiking neurons (presumptive spiny neurons) in L4 have a much lower connection probability (~11%) with LGN neurons compared to neighboring SINs.
source: By contrast to the profuse TC connectivity seen in L4 SINs, regular-spiking neurons (presumptive spiny neurons), found just above or below an L4 SIN that is connected to an LGN neuron (within 150 microns in the same vertical penetration) have a much lower connection probability (~11%, compare Figures 5A and 3D)
evidence: This is based on the connectivity data shown in Figures 5A and 3D.

claim: >80% of regular-spiking non-SINs in L4 of rabbit V1 are simple cells.
source: We have previously shown that > 80% of such regular-spiking non-SINs in L4 of rabbit V1 are simple cells (Zhuang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the same authors.

claim: In L4 of cat V1, simple cells receive a highly selective input from LGN TC neurons that depends on retinotopic alignment and spatiotemporal RF match, while the inputs to fast-spiking neurons are less selective.
source: Similarly, in L4 of cat V1, simple cells receive a highly selective input from LGN TC neurons that depends on retinotopic alignment and spatiotemporal RF match, while the inputs to fast-spiking neurons are less selective (Alonso et al., 2001; Reid and Alonso, 1995; Sedigh-Sarvestani et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In somatosensory barrel cortex of rats, regular-spiking L4 neurons receive input from ventrobasal TC neurons at a much lower probability than do L4 fast-spike neurons.
source: Findings in somatosensory barrel cortex of rats are similar, where regular-spiking L4 neurons receive input from ventrobasal TC neurons at a much lower probability than do L4 fast-spike neurons (Bruno and Simons, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The RFs of putative fast-spike GABAergic inhibitory interneurons in rabbit V1 form a uniform class of 'complex' cells, with spatially overlapping ON and OFF subfields and little or no orientation or directional selectivity.
source: These results, as well as previous results in rabbit V1, indicate that the RFs of putative fast-spike GABAergic inhibitory interneurons form a uniform class of 'complex' cells, with spatially overlapping ON and OFF subfields and little or no orientation or directional selectivity.
evidence: This is based on the current data and previous work in rabbit V1.

claim: In cat V1, the RF properties of fast-spike interneurons are more heterogeneous than in rabbit.
source: In the cat, however, the RF properties of fast-spike interneurons are more heterogeneous.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent discussion and citations.

claim: Hirsch et al., 2003 found that four of ten neurons with smooth dendrites and presumptive fast-spiking properties had RFs with spatially overlapping ON/OFF subfields and little orientation/direction selectivity, while the remaining six had classic 'simple' RFs.
source: Thus, Hirsch et al., 2003 recorded intracellularly from 10 neurons with smooth dendrites and presumptive fast-spiking properties. They found that four of these cells had RFs that closely resembled the SINs of this study (spatially overlapping ON/OFF subfields, little orientation/direction selectivity), and the remaining 6 of these cells had classic 'simple' RFs.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited study.

claim: Nowak et al., 2008 found that some fast-spike cells were very broadly tuned to orientation.
source: Similarly, Nowak et al., 2008 recorded intracellularly and used cluster analysis to segregate cell types based on electrophysiological and RF properties. They found that some fast-spike cells were very broadly tuned to orientation
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited study.

claim: Cardin et al., 2007 found only small differences between fast-spike and regular-spike cell classes in cat L4.
source: By contrast, Cardin et al., 2007 found only small differences between fast-spike and regular-spike cell classes in cat L4.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited study.

claim: The SINs found in rabbit V1 may have their counterparts in feline V1, but the well-tuned fast-spike interneurons with 'simple' RFs found in cat L4 are not found in rabbit V1.
source: Thus, it seems that the SINs found in rabbit V1 (Swadlow and Weyand, 1987; Swadlow, 1988; Zhuang et al., 2013; this study) may have their counterparts in feline V1, but that the well-tuned fast-spike interneurons with 'simple' RFs found in cat L4 are not found in rabbit V1.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of findings across species.

claim: In layer 2/3 of mouse, inhibitory interneurons of multiple classes were found to be very broadly tuned to orientation and a number of other stimulus features.
source: In layer 2/3 of mouse, however, inhibitory interneurons of multiple classes were found to be very broadly tuned to orientation and a number of other stimulus features (Kerlin et al., 2010; Sohya et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The promiscuous connectivity between LGN concentric neurons and retinotopically-aligned L4 SINs is reminiscent of the 'complete transmission line' between nodes of a network described by Griffith, 1963.
source: The promiscuous connectivity seen here between LGN concentric neurons and retinotopically-aligned L4 SINs is reminiscent of the 'complete transmission line' between nodes of a network, described by Griffith, 1963, and elaborated by Abeles, 1991 (who adapted such a network as the basis of his 'synfire chain').
evidence: This is a comparison to theoretical network models from cited work.

claim: In complete transmission line networks, each member of one node excites each member of the successive node via richly convergent/divergent synaptic connectivity.
source: In such networks, each member of one node excites each member of the successive node via richly convergent/divergent synaptic connectivity.
evidence: This is a description of the theoretical network model.

claim: Neurons in the output node of complete transmission line networks are expected to show high sensitivity but decreased ability to discriminate among selective properties of the input elements.
source: Neurons in the output node (SINs, in this case) are expected to show high sensitivity (because of their profuse inputs), but they suffer a decreased ability to discriminate among any selective properties of the input elements.
evidence: This is a prediction from the theoretical network model.

claim: L4 SINs in rabbit V1 are more sensitive to stimulus contrast than are L4 simple cells.
source: Thus, these cells are more sensitive to stimulus contrast than are L4 simple cells and have a spatial RF that consists of spatially overlapping ON and OFF subfields (despite the fact that the concentric LGN input cells responded to either ON or OFF in the RF center).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Zhuang et al., 2013).

claim: L4 SINs are more broadly tuned to spatial and temporal frequency, stimulus direction and orientation than are simple cells of V1.
source: Moreover, they are more broadly tuned to a number of stimulus parameters (spatial and temporal frequency, stimulus direction and orientation) than are simple cells of V1.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Zhuang et al., 2013).

claim: SINs of somatosensory barrel cortex are synaptically connected to neurons in ventrobasal thalamus in a richly divergent/convergent manner.
source: Similarly, SINs of somatosensory barrel cortex are synaptically connected to neurons in ventrobasal thalamus in a richly divergent/convergent manner.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent citations.

claim: Cross-correlation studies reveal a connection probability of ~2/3 between SINs in an L4 barrel and TC neurons of the topographically aligned thalamic barreloid.
source: In that system, cross-correlation studies reveal a connection probability of ~2/3 between SINs in an L4 barrel, and TC neurons of the topographically aligned thalamic barreloid (Bruno and Simons, 2002; Swadlow et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SINs of S1 barrel cortex display lowest thresholds to whisker stimulation of any neurons found in the S1 barrel.
source: Thus, they display 'high sensitivity', showing lowest thresholds to whisker stimulation of any neurons found in the S1 barrel, and they show very broad temporal and directional tuning (Swadlow, 1989; Swadlow, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The lack of directional tuning in SINs of L4 barrel cortex is thought to result from the highly convergent input from multiple neurons in their aligned thalamic barreloid that display different directional preferences.
source: The lack of directional tuning in SINs of L4 barrel cortex is thought to result from the highly convergent input to these from multiple neurons in their aligned thalamic barreloid that display different directional preferences (Swadlow and Gusev, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and represents an inference about mechanism.

claim: TC pruning during development is likely to be more pronounced in excitatory than in fast-spike inhibitory cortical neurons leading to differences in their RF selectivity.
source: They suggest that TC pruning during development is likely to be more pronounced in excitatory than in fast-spike inhibitory cortical neurons leading to differences in their RF selectivity (Alonso and Swadlow, 2005; Cardin et al., 2007; Bruno and Simons, 2002).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The connectivity difference between excitatory and fast-spike inhibitory neurons is likely to generalize across sensory systems and species.
source: This connectivity difference is likely to generalize across sensory systems and species.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the current findings and previous work.

claim: In cat visual cortex, each thalamic afferent makes connection with an estimated 15 to 33% of retinotopically aligned cortical excitatory neurons.
source: For example, in both visual and somatosensory cortex, each thalamic afferent is known to make connection with a small percentage of cortical excitatory neurons that are retinotopically or somatotopically aligned, a percentage that is estimated to be ~15 to 33% in cat visual cortex (Alonso et al., 2001; Sedigh-Sarvestani et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In rabbit visual cortex, each thalamic afferent makes connection with 11% of retinotopically aligned cortical excitatory neurons.
source: 11% in rabbit visual cortex (as shown here, Figure 5A)
evidence: This is based on the data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In rat barrel cortex, each thalamic afferent makes connection with 37% of somatotopically aligned cortical excitatory neurons.
source: and 37% in rat barrel cortex (Bruno and Simons, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In both visual and somatosensory cortex, each thalamic afferent makes a higher percentage of connections with fast-spike inhibitory than excitatory neurons.
source: Also, in both visual and somatosensory cortex, each thalamic afferent makes a higher percentage of connections with fast-spike inhibitory than excitatory neurons (Swadlow and Gusev, 2002, Alonso and Swadlow, 2005; Bruno and Simons, 2002; Sedigh-Sarvestani et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: All estimates of connection probability reported in the past failed to take into account the laminar specificity of the axonal arbor from the thalamic afferent and the presence of L4 cortical neurons that may receive weak or no direct thalamic input.
source: While these similarities in TC connectivity are well known, all estimates of connection probability reported in the past failed to take into account the laminar specificity of the axonal arbor from the thalamic afferent and the presence of L4 cortical neurons that may receive weak or no direct thalamic input.
evidence: This is a critical observation about limitations of previous studies.

claim: When the laminar specificity of the axonal arbor is taken into account, each thalamic afferent makes connection with nearly all of the first-order (short-latency) fast-spike inhibitory neurons that are within reach of the axonal arbor regardless of the response properties of the LGN and cortical neurons.
source: Remarkably, our results indicate that, when the laminar specificity of the axonal arbor is taken into account, each thalamic afferent makes connection with nearly all of the first-order (short-latency) fast-spike inhibitory neurons that are within reach of the axonal arbor regardless of the response properties of the LGN and cortical neurons.
evidence: This is based on the data showing 40/41 cases of connectivity when the three rules are satisfied.

claim: The three rules of synaptic connectivity predict connection probability with a high level of precision that is not yet possible for any other TC circuit in any other species.
source: The 'three rules' of synaptic connectivity that we describe are both necessary and sufficient for predicting connectivity between LGN neurons and L4 SINs (40/41 cases, Figure 4C). Together, they predict connection probability with a surprising high level of precision that is not yet possible for any other TC circuit in any other species.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and precision of the current findings.

claim: Nonselective pooling of thalamic afferents can be amplified by nonselective pooling of inhibitory neurons connecting to the same cortical excitatory neuron.
source: This nonselective pooling of thalamic afferents can be amplified by nonselective pooling of inhibitory neurons connecting to the same cortical excitatory neuron (Taylor et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The promiscuous, highly convergent TC connectivity onto retinotopically/topographically aligned L4 fast-spike inhibitory interneurons may be a general feature of sensory neocortex.
source: We propose that the observed promiscuous, highly convergent TC connectivity onto retinotopically/topographically aligned L4 fast-spike inhibitory interneurons may be a general feature of sensory neocortex
evidence: This is a speculation based on the current findings and previous work across systems.

claim: The promiscuous TC connectivity plays a causal role in generating the fast, sensitive, broadly tuned, and powerful feed-forward TC inhibition of excitatory neurons within L4.
source: and that this feature plays a causal role in generating the fast, sensitive, broadly tuned, and powerful feed-forward TC inhibition of excitatory neurons that is seen within L4 (Bagnall et al., 2011; Cruikshank et al., 2007; Cruikshank et al., 2010; Gabernet et al., 2005; Hull et al., 2009; Miller et al., 2001b; Swadlow, 1995; Swadlow, 2003; Taylor et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequences of the connectivity pattern, supported by citations.

claim: All animal procedures were conducted with the approval of the University of Connecticut Animal Care and Use Committee in accordance with the National Institutes of Health guidelines.
source: All animal procedures were conducted with the approval of the University of Connecticut Animal Care and Use Committee in accordance with the National Institutes of Health guidelines.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: A concentric array of seven independently movable electrodes was placed within the LGN with electrode separation of ~200 μm.
source: A concentric array of seven independently movable electrodes was placed within the LGN (electrode separation ~200 um, Swadlow et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental methods.

claim: Recordings were made using fine-diameter (40 micron) quartz-insulated platinum/tungsten electrodes tapered and sharpened to a fine tip.
source: Recordings were made using fine-diameter (40 micron) quartz-insulated platinum/tungsten electrodes tapered and sharpened to a fine tip.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental methods.

claim: Extracellular single-unit recordings were recorded from the retinotopically-aligned region of V1 using either 16-channel silicon probes with 100 microns vertical spacing or single electrodes moved through the depth of the cortex.
source: Extracellular single-unit recordings were recorded from the retinotopically-aligned region of V1 using either 16-channel silicon probes with 100 microns vertical spacing (NeuroNexus Technologies) or the same fine-diameter single electrodes, that were moved through the depth of the cortex.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental methods.

claim: All electrophysiological activity was recorded in the awake state.
source: All electrophysiological activity was recorded in the awake state (e.g. Bereshpolova et al., 2007; Bereshpolova et al., 2019; Bezdudnaya et al., 2006; Zhuang et al., 2013)
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental methods with supporting citations.

claim: Spontaneous spike trains were used in cross-correlation analyses to avoid stimulus-induced correlations.
source: In order to avoid stimulus-induced correlations, spontaneous spike trains were used in these analyses (e.g. Bereshpolova et al., 2011; Bereshpolova et al., 2019; Swadlow and Gusev, 2001; Swadlow and Gusev, 2002; Zhuang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the methodological approach with supporting citations.

claim: Visual stimuli were presented on a CRT monitor with mean luminance 48 cd/m2 and refresh rate 160 Hz.
source: All stimuli were generated using custom-made program (Visual C++, DirectX 7), and presented on a CRT monitor (Nec MultiSync 40 × 30 cm, mean luminance 48 cd/m2, refresh rate 160 Hz).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental methods.

claim: RFs were mapped using sparse noise made of white and black squares (0.5–2° in a grid of 30 × 22 degrees) in a pseudorandom sequence.
source: RFs were mapped using sparse noise (Jones and Palmer, 1987), made of white and black squares (0.5–2° in a grid of 30 × 22 degrees) in a pseudorandom sequence
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental methods with citation.

claim: Identification of cortical layers was based on the reversal point of the field potential generated by a diffuse flash stimulus.
source: Identification of cortical layers was based on the reversal point of the field potential generated by a diffuse flash stimulus (Stoelzel et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental methods with citation.

claim: Monosynaptic connection was inferred from the presence of a significant peak in the probability of SIN firing at intervals of 1–4 ms in cross-correlograms.
source: Monosynaptic connection was inferred from the presence of a significant peak in the probability of SIN firing at intervals of 1–4 ms (reflecting the presynaptic axonal conduction time, the synaptic delay, and the rise-time of postsynaptic firing).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the methodological criteria for inferring connectivity.

claim: A peak in a cross-correlogram was defined as significant when at least two of three successive bins (0.1 ms bin width) in the peak exceeded the 0.01 confidence level.
source: A peak in a cross-correlogram was defined as significant when at least two of three successive bins (0.1 ms bin width) in the peak exceeded the 0.01 confidence level.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the statistical criteria used.
